questions.text: What does multiversioning mean in PostgreSQL?

answers.text: The ability for multiple versions of the same row to exist
Storing multiple copies of the entire database
Automatically creating multiple indexes
Running multiple PostgreSQL instances at the same time

questions.explanation: The material defines multiversioning as the existence of multiple versions of the same row.

questions.text: Which statements about row versions are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Multiple versions of one row can exist
Versions differ by their period of validity
Transaction numbers are used as the time markers
Transaction numbers are assigned in increasing order
Each row version must be stored in a separate table

questions.explanation: The course associates the lifetime of a row version with transaction identifiers, which are assigned in increasing order.

questions.text: What does a transaction work with when MVCC is used?

answers.text: A data snapshot — a consistent view at a particular moment
Only the physical contents of files at the current millisecond
Only data modified by the transaction itself
A backup copy of the cluster

questions.explanation: A snapshot is a consistent view of data that determines which row versions a transaction can see.

questions.text: What primarily distinguishes PostgreSQL isolation levels in the context of MVCC?

answers.text: When the data snapshot is created
The data-page size
The WAL format
The number of allowed tables

questions.explanation: The summary of the material explicitly notes that isolation levels differ in when a snapshot is created.

questions.text: How does PostgreSQL handle the Read Uncommitted isolation level?

answers.text: It effectively behaves as Read Committed
It behaves as Serializable
It completely disables MVCC
It is the default isolation level

questions.explanation: Read Uncommitted does not have separate semantics in PostgreSQL and behaves like Read Committed.

questions.text: Which isolation level is the PostgreSQL default?

answers.text: Read Committed
Read Uncommitted
Repeatable Read
Serializable

questions.explanation: The course explicitly identifies Read Committed as PostgreSQL's default isolation level.

questions.text: When is a data snapshot created at Read Committed?

answers.text: At the start of each SQL statement
Once when the server starts
Only at COMMIT
Once for the entire client session

questions.explanation: At Read Committed, a new snapshot is built for each SQL statement.

questions.text: Why can two identical SELECT statements in one Read Committed transaction return different results?

answers.text: Each statement gets a new snapshot and can see changes committed between the queries
PostgreSQL randomly selects row versions
Read Committed does not use snapshots
The first SELECT always blocks the second

questions.explanation: Because the snapshot is built at the start of each statement, a later query can see newly committed data.

questions.text: When is the snapshot created at Repeatable Read?

answers.text: When the transaction's first statement is executed
Before every individual statement
Only after COMMIT
Every time a new table is accessed

questions.explanation: The material describes this as creation of a snapshot at the start of a transaction, more precisely when its first statement is executed.

questions.text: Which statements about PostgreSQL Repeatable Read are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: All queries in the transaction use one snapshot
Queries in the transaction see the same consistent view of data
The level is convenient for reports made up of several queries
A new snapshot must be created for every statement

questions.explanation: Repeatable Read keeps one snapshot throughout the transaction, which makes it suitable, for example, for multi-step reports.

questions.text: What is true of Serializable? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It provides full isolation
An application can be written as if the transaction were running alone
Some transactions can be aborted
The application must be able to retry aborted transactions
It guarantees that no transaction will ever be aborted

questions.explanation: Serializable provides the strictest isolation, but the price is that transactions can be aborted and must be retried by the application.

questions.text: Why does multiversioning require periodic cleanup?

answers.text: Because old row versions eventually become unnecessary
Because every SELECT damages pages
Because MVCC deletes indexes
Because snapshots cannot be used more than once

questions.explanation: MVCC leaves historical row versions behind; when no transaction can need them anymore, they should be cleaned up.

source.locator: Section on cleaning up old versions

questions.text: How can old row versions be cleaned up? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: By background processes
Manually with VACUUM
Only when the server restarts
Only with DROP TABLE

questions.explanation: The material mentions both automatic background cleanup and the possibility of running it manually with VACUUM.

questions.text: How do long transactions and long-running queries affect cleanup?

answers.text: They can hold back the cleanup horizon and prevent removal of old row versions
They automatically remove all old versions
They disable MVCC for other sessions
They force PostgreSQL to immediately run a full VACUUM

questions.explanation: An old transaction may still need old versions, so the cleanup horizon cannot advance beyond it.

questions.text: What can result from failing to clean up historical versions in time? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Tables consume unnecessary space
Indexes grow
Finding current versions can become slower
PostgreSQL stops supporting transactions

questions.explanation: Accumulation of obsolete versions increases the size of tables and indexes and makes work with current versions less efficient.

source.locator: Section on the consequences of delayed cleanup

questions.text: How does MVCC affect the amount of locking required?

answers.text: It allows PostgreSQL to use only the minimum necessary locking
It requires locking the whole database for every read
It completely forbids all locks
It uses locks only for SELECT

questions.explanation: One advantage of multiversioning is the reduced need for locking, which improves concurrency.

source.locator: Section on the role of locks with MVCC

questions.text: What happens during an ordinary row read in PostgreSQL?

answers.text: The read blocks neither readers nor writers
The row is locked against any changes until the end of the session
The entire table is locked
SELECT always waits for all other transactions to finish

questions.explanation: Ordinary reads under MVCC do not need to lock rows against reading or modification.

questions.text: What happens when a row is modified?

answers.text: The row is locked against other modifications but remains available for reading
The row becomes unavailable even to SELECT
The entire cluster is locked
No lock is taken even for competing modifications

questions.explanation: Modifying a row conflicts with other modifications of that same row, but does not prevent an ordinary read.

questions.text: When can a transaction wait for a row lock to be released?

answers.text: When it tries to modify a row already modified by another unfinished transaction
During any ordinary SELECT
When reading the system catalog
At every BEGIN

questions.explanation: A conflict occurs between concurrent changes to one row: the second writer must wait until the first writer's situation is resolved.

questions.text: What does PostgreSQL use table-level locks for? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: To prevent a table from being altered or dropped while another incompatible operation is using it
To restrict reads during some table rebuild or movement operations
To make every SELECT execute sequentially
To replace MVCC

questions.explanation: In addition to row locks, there are higher-level locks needed to coordinate operations involving the structure and physical state of tables.

questions.text: What is true about the lifetime of locks? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: They can be acquired automatically as needed
Some locks can be acquired manually
They are normally released automatically when the transaction ends
A lock acquired after a SAVEPOINT can be released by rolling back to that savepoint
All locks persist until PostgreSQL is restarted

questions.explanation: The material associates the normal lifetime of locks with a transaction; when rolling back to a savepoint, locks acquired after that savepoint can also be released.

questions.text: What is the best short description of reader/writer interaction under PostgreSQL MVCC?

answers.text: Writers do not block readers, and readers do not block anyone
Every reader blocks all writers
Every writer blocks all reads of the table
Reading and writing can never happen concurrently

questions.explanation: This wording is presented on the topic's summary slide as one of the key consequences of MVCC.

questions.text: Which data is included in a simplified PostgreSQL snapshot model? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The number of the last committed transaction when the snapshot was created
The list of transactions active when the snapshot was created
A complete physical copy of all database pages
A list of all SQL queries executed since server startup

questions.explanation: A snapshot does not physically copy data. In the lesson model, it is described by a few numbers: the boundary of committed transactions and the list of transactions that were still active.

questions.text: Which statements about transaction status and rollback are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Transaction statuses are stored in service files under PGDATA/pg_xact
On commit or abort, it is sufficient to change the transaction status
On ROLLBACK, PostgreSQL must physically restore every modified page to its previous state
Versions created by an aborted transaction can remain physically present, but other transactions do not consider them visible

questions.explanation: The material describes the commit log (clog): transaction status is recorded separately, so aborting a transaction does not require physically undoing all changes; versions from an aborted transaction are ignored according to its status.
